texts.0: SP did not know the spin prevention and spin recovery procedures by heart, due to incomplete study of the boldface before the sortie. SP omitted and reversed steps of the published sequence, kept power applied with the controls displaced, and allowed the spin to continue through additional turns. IP took the aircraft and executed the recovery. The procedure was not applied in any recognisable order.
texts.1: SP recalled the recovery procedure only in fragments, due to weak memorisation of the boldface items. SP hesitated after the entry and applied the steps out of order, completing the sequence only after repeated verbal prompting by the IP. The delay allowed the spin to develop well past the incipient phase, at the limit of an acceptable recovery.
texts.2: SP applied the recovery procedure with an initial hesitation, due to incomplete memorisation of the sequence. SP paused before setting power to idle, then recognised the omission and completed the remaining steps in the correct order without any prompt. The delay cost part of a turn but the recovery was self-initiated and effective.
texts.3: SP knew the spin prevention and spin recovery procedures by heart and applied them without hesitation. SP identified the spin condition immediately and executed the published steps in the correct order and at the correct time. The aircraft was returned to controlled flight promptly on every attempt.
texts.4: SP recited and executed the recovery procedure flawlessly, with no pause between recognition and action. SP applied each step at the exact point required and verbalised the sequence while flying it. Recovery was immediate and identical on repeated entries.
texts.marginal: SP knew the recovery procedure and applied it within standards, but the recall was still recited rather than automatic and the first step came a beat late on each entry. This tendency did not affect the outcome, yet under a real departure it leaves little margin. SP is expected to bring the boldface to full automatic recall for the next sortie.

texts_at.0: SP worked through the spin prevention and spin recovery sequence with the IP talking through each boldface item in turn, rather than recalling the sequence as a single memorized block. This is the first time the procedure has been flown against an actual departure rather than rehearsed on the ground, and the recall is not yet automatic. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to recall the sequence as a whole on the next entry rather than one prompted step at a time.
texts_at.1: SP recalled the spin prevention and spin recovery procedure and worked through the published sequence without omitting or reversing any step, due to a boldface that was still recited item by item rather than run from memory as a whole. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to consolidate the sequence into a single recalled block rather than a chain of individual items.
texts_at.2: SP applied the recovery procedure in the correct order on every entry, due to a boldface that was solid but still checked silently against memory before each step was actioned. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to reduce that mental check so the sequence is actioned as it is recalled.
texts_at.3: SP knew the recovery procedure by heart and applied every step without hesitation, due to a habit of pausing a beat between recognising the spin and starting the sequence rather than beginning it in the same instant. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to close that beat so recognition and the first action arrive together.

texts_above.1: SP worked through the spin recovery sequence and completed every boldface step, correcting the order of one step after a single verbal call from the IP rather than needing the sequence demonstrated again. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recalled the spin recovery procedure from memory and applied every step in the published order on both entries, with no hesitation and no re-ordering. Verbalising the sequence while flying it would sharpen the recall further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good procedure recall.
texts_above.3: SP recalled and applied the full recovery sequence without a single omission across all entries, moving through the boldface as one continuous action rather than a checked list. The only refinement available was to verbalise the sequence as it is flown. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good procedure recall.
texts_above.4: SP recited and executed the recovery procedure with no pause between recognition and action on every entry, applying each step at the exact point required. The technique is already sound; nothing in the sequence needs to change. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent command of the boldface.

error_modes.label: CONTROL INPUTS DURING RECOVERY (SMOOTH AND SOLID)

texts.0: SP did not make smooth and solid stick movements during the recovery, due to a startle response at the spin entry. SP applied abrupt and reversed inputs, released the controls before the rotation stopped and re-entered the autorotation. IP had to take the controls and hold them in the recovery position to stop the spin.
texts.1: SP made rushed and uneven stick movements during the recovery, due to a startle response that persisted after the entry. SP relaxed the input before the rotation had fully stopped and re-applied it only after being told to hold the controls in position. Recovery was achieved at the limit of the acceptable, with rotation continuing longer than required.
texts.2: SP made the recovery inputs less smoothly than required, due to a brief startle at the departure. SP moved the stick abruptly on the first application, recognised the roughness and settled into a steady and solid hold for the remainder of the recovery without any comment from the IP. The aircraft recovered with only a slight increase in rotation.
texts.3: SP made smooth and solid stick movements throughout the recovery. SP applied the inputs positively, held them until the rotation stopped and then released them progressively as flying speed returned. Control handling was steady on each entry.
texts.4: SP made precise, smooth and firm stick movements with no trace of startle at the entry. SP held each input exactly as long as required and blended the release into the dive recovery without any control reversal. Handling was consistent and unhurried on all repetitions.
texts.marginal: SP made solid stick movements within standards, but the first input after each entry was still applied more quickly than the technique calls for. The tendency was self-limited and did not degrade the recovery. SP is expected to smooth the initial application on the next spin sortie.

texts_at.0: SP made the recovery control inputs with the IP guiding the first application hand over hand, since the startle response at this first exposure to the departure still overwhelms an unpracticed grip on the controls. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to make the initial application without that hands-on guidance on the next entry.
texts_at.1: SP made the recovery inputs smooth and solid on each entry, due to a startle response at the departure that still produced a firmer first application of the stick before the hold settled. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to soften that first application so the whole input reads as one smooth movement from the start.
texts_at.2: SP held the recovery controls steady and solid through the rotation, due to a startle reaction that eased only a beat after the initial input rather than being absent from it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to manage the startle before the hand reaches the stick so the very first movement is already smooth.
texts_at.3: SP made smooth and solid stick movements throughout the recovery on every entry, due to a grip that stayed slightly firmer than necessary through the hold before easing for the release. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to relax the grip once the anti-spin inputs are set.

texts_above.1: SP applied the recovery inputs and stopped the rotation without the controls being taken, the first movement still showing the startle response before the hold settled. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP made the recovery inputs smoothly and firmly on both entries, absorbing the startle at the departure without any trace of it reaching the controls. Holding the input for a fraction longer before beginning the release would make the transition to the dive recovery cleaner still. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound control handling.
texts_above.3: SP applied smooth, firm and consistent stick movements on every entry, with the startle response fully managed before the hand reached the controls. The technique is already sound; nothing in the input sizing or timing needs to change. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to disciplined control application.
texts_above.4: SP made precise, smooth and unhurried recovery inputs with no trace of startle at any entry, holding each application exactly as long as required and blending the release into the dive recovery without a single reversal. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional control handling.

texts.0: SP did not recover the aircraft with minimum loss of altitude, due to late recognition of the spin and a slow application of the recovery steps. SP allowed the rotation to continue and then held a shallow dive angle far longer than required, losing altitude well beyond what the maneuver demands and approaching the recovery floor. IP intervened and terminated the maneuver.
texts.1: SP recovered the aircraft with excessive loss of altitude, due to a delayed dive recovery after the rotation stopped. SP left the nose low and accepted a prolonged descent, initiating the pull only after being prompted by the IP. Altitude loss reached the limit of the acceptable margin above the recovery floor.
texts.2: SP lost more altitude than necessary during the recovery, due to a slow transition from the anti-spin inputs to the dive recovery. SP recognised the increasing descent, promptly raised the nose to the horizon and stopped the altitude loss without any prompting. The remaining margin above the recovery floor stayed comfortable.
texts.3: SP recovered the aircraft with minimum loss of altitude. SP stopped the rotation promptly and made an immediate but controlled dive recovery to level flight. Altitude loss was consistent with the technique and the recovery floor was never a factor.
texts.4: SP recovered the aircraft with the least practicable loss of altitude on every entry. SP transitioned from the anti-spin inputs to the dive recovery with no dead time and levelled the aircraft with a large margin above the recovery floor. Altitude loss was repeatable and minimal.
texts.marginal: SP recovered within standards but the altitude loss trended toward the upper end of what the maneuver requires on each entry. The technique worked, yet the margin above the recovery floor was smaller than it needs to be. SP is expected to tighten the transition from rotation stop to dive recovery on the next sortie.

texts_at.0: SP stopped the rotation and recovered from the dive with the IP calling each step of the sequence in turn, since flying the recovery to a full stop of rotation is being attempted for the first time rather than talked through on the ground. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to fly the same recovery from the verbal cues alone before the next departure is entered.
texts_at.1: SP recovered the aircraft with an altitude loss of about 300 feet against the briefed recovery profile, at the outer edge of the standard, due to a dive recovery started promptly but flown at a slightly shallow pull before the aircraft reached level flight. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to increase the pull rate once the rotation has stopped so the recovery closes sooner.
texts_at.2: SP stopped the rotation and recovered from the dive with the altitude loss held to about 250 feet, clear of the recovery floor, due to a brief pause between the rotation stopping and the pull beginning rather than the two actions running together. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to start the pull the instant the rotation stops rather than after confirming it has stopped.
texts_at.3: SP recovered the aircraft with the altitude loss contained within about 150 feet on every entry, due to a dive angle held a fraction longer than necessary before the pull was applied. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to trim the dive angle held so the pull begins as soon as flying speed allows it.

texts_above.1: SP stopped the rotation and made the dive recovery to level flight, holding the altitude loss to approximately 280 feet above the recovery floor. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP stopped the rotation promptly and made an immediate, controlled dive recovery on every entry, keeping the altitude loss well inside what the recovery floor allows. Starting the pull the instant the rotation stops, rather than a moment after, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid recovery technique.
texts_above.3: SP transitioned from the anti-spin inputs to the dive recovery with almost no dead time on every entry, leaving a wide and repeatable margin above the recovery floor. The only refinement available was to shorten the dive angle held before the pull is applied. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed energy management in the recovery.
texts_above.4: SP recovered the aircraft with the least practicable loss of altitude on every entry, transitioning from the anti-spin inputs to the dive recovery with no dead time and levelling with a large margin above the recovery floor each time. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to outstanding recovery discipline.

texts.0: SP allowed the appearance of a secondary stall during the dive recovery and did not take the proper action, due to an aggressive pull applied before flying speed had been regained. SP maintained back stick pressure through the buffet and let the aircraft depart again. IP took the controls to unload the aircraft and complete the recovery.
texts.1: SP allowed a secondary stall to develop during the dive recovery, due to an early and heavy pull after the rotation stopped. SP recognised the buffet only after the IP called it and then reduced the back pressure to unload the wing. The corrective action was correct but late, and the entry into the secondary stall was clear.
texts.2: SP approached a secondary stall during the dive recovery, due to a pull initiated slightly before adequate flying speed. SP felt the onset of the buffet, immediately relaxed the back pressure and completed the recovery at a reduced load factor without any input from the IP. No full secondary stall developed.
texts.3: SP did not allow the appearance of a secondary stall. SP waited for flying speed before applying back pressure and completed the dive recovery at a load factor well clear of the buffet. The wing remained unstalled throughout the recovery.
texts.4: SP kept the aircraft entirely clear of any secondary stall on every recovery, with no trace of buffet. SP judged the point of adequate flying speed accurately and blended the pull so that the load factor stayed comfortably below the onset. Angle of attack management was precise throughout.
texts.marginal: SP avoided any secondary stall and stayed within standards, but the back pressure during the dive recovery was applied close to the buffet margin on each attempt. Nothing developed, yet the technique leaves little room if the recovery is flown at a lower speed. SP is expected to delay the pull slightly and increase the margin next time.

texts_at.0: SP flew the dive recovery with the IP calling the point at which back pressure could be applied without risking a secondary stall, since judging that margin from the buffet alone is not yet a skill this early in spin training. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to judge that margin from the aircraft's own feel on the next sortie rather than from the call.
texts_at.1: SP did not allow a secondary stall to develop on any entry, due to back pressure applied close to the buffet margin before it was relaxed to the load factor the recovery requires. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to wait for a clearer confirmation of flying speed before applying the same rate of back pressure.
texts_at.2: SP kept the dive recovery clear of any secondary stall on every entry, due to a pull started a fraction before adequate flying speed was fully confirmed, easing at the first sign of buffet onset. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to confirm flying speed before committing to the same rate of back pressure.
texts_at.3: SP did not allow the appearance of a secondary stall on any recovery, due to a load factor held close to, but still clear of, the buffet margin through the pull. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to build in a wider load margin before the buffet is even approached.

texts_above.1: SP kept the dive recovery clear of a secondary stall, easing the back pressure at the first sign of buffet after being told to wait for flying speed on the entry. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP kept every dive recovery clear of a secondary stall, waiting for flying speed before applying back pressure and completing each pull at a load factor away from the buffet. Delaying the pull by a further beat on the fastest entries would widen the margin still. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady angle-of-attack management.
texts_above.3: SP judged the point of adequate flying speed accurately on every recovery and blended the pull so the load factor stayed comfortably below the buffet onset each time. The technique is already sound; nothing in the timing of the pull needs to change. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to consistently accurate stall-margin management.
texts_above.4: SP kept the aircraft entirely clear of any secondary stall on every recovery, with no trace of buffet and angle-of-attack management that was precise throughout each pull. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary stall-margin discipline.

texts.0: SP exceeded the aircraft limits during the recovery, due to an unmonitored dive and a late, heavy pull. SP allowed the airspeed and the load factor to build past the published limits with no attempt to reduce power or unload. IP took the aircraft to arrest the acceleration and the exceedance had to be reported.
texts.1: SP took the aircraft to the published limits during the dive recovery, due to a nose-low attitude held too long with power applied. SP reduced the pull and checked the acceleration only after the IP called the airspeed. The limits were reached rather than exceeded, but only because of the verbal intervention.
texts.2: SP allowed the airspeed and load factor to increase toward the published limits during the dive recovery, due to a late reduction of the dive angle. SP noticed the trend on the instruments, raised the nose and eased the pull in time, keeping the values clear of the limits without any prompt. The margin remained adequate throughout.
texts.3: SP did not exceed the aircraft limits at any stage of the entry or the recovery. SP managed power, dive angle and load factor so that airspeed and G stayed within the published values. All parameters remained inside limits on each repetition.
texts.4: SP kept the aircraft well inside every published limit throughout the maneuver, with wide margins on airspeed and load factor. SP anticipated the acceleration in the dive and controlled it before it became a factor. Limit management was consistent on all entries.
texts.marginal: SP stayed within the aircraft limits, but airspeed in the dive recovery reached the upper part of the acceptable band on each attempt. No limit was approached closely enough to affect the grade, yet the trend is consistent. SP is expected to control the dive angle earlier so the margin to the limits increases.

texts_at.0: SP flew the dive recovery with the IP calling the airspeed and G as the pull developed, since managing power, dive angle and load factor together has not yet been practiced without that running commentary. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to monitor airspeed and G independently on the next entry rather than from the call.
texts_at.1: SP did not exceed the aircraft limits on any recovery, with the airspeed reaching about 20 knots from the reference during the pull, at the outer edge of the standard, due to a pull rate that took the airspeed and load factor close to the published values before the increase was checked. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to ease the pull earlier in the recovery so the limits are approached with more margin.
texts_at.2: SP kept airspeed and load factor inside the published limits on every recovery, with the airspeed reaching about 15 knots from the reference, due to a dive angle allowed to develop slightly before the reduction began, closing the margin more than the technique calls for. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to start reducing the dive angle earlier so the limits are never closely approached.
texts_at.3: SP did not exceed the aircraft limits at any stage of the recovery, with the airspeed no more than about 10 knots off the reference, due to a pull sized close to what the situation needed without a wider margin built in. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to size the pull with a larger buffer against the published limits.

texts_above.1: SP kept the aircraft inside the published limits through the recovery, easing the pull once the airspeed and load factor were called approaching the published values. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP managed power, dive angle and load factor so that airspeed and G stayed clear of the published limits on every recovery, controlling the acceleration in the dive before it became a factor. Reading the trend a moment earlier would widen the margin further still. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable limit management.
texts_above.3: SP anticipated the acceleration in the dive on every recovery and controlled it well before the published limits could be approached, with the pull sized precisely to the attitude and energy state. The only refinement available was to begin the reduction fractionally earlier still on the steepest entries. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good energy control.
texts_above.4: SP flew every recovery with a wide and consistent margin to the load and airspeed limits while still resolving the attitude at the first opportunity, with control inputs sized precisely to the attitude presented. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior limit management.

texts.0: SP did not stabilise the aircraft at the recovery altitude, due to an unmonitored pitch attitude after the dive recovery. SP allowed the aircraft to porpoise through the target altitude and settled more than 300 feet away from it without recognising the deviation. IP took the aircraft to establish level flight.
texts.1: SP levelled off approximately 300 feet from the intended recovery altitude, due to a late check of the altimeter after the dive recovery. SP held the incorrect altitude and only started the correction after the IP pointed out the deviation. The recovery to the assigned altitude was slow.
texts.2: SP overshot the intended recovery altitude by between 150 and 300 feet, due to a nose-low attitude held slightly too long. SP identified the deviation on the altimeter and returned to the assigned altitude promptly and without prompting. Level flight was then maintained accurately.
texts.3: SP established level flight within 150 feet of the intended recovery altitude. SP checked the altimeter immediately after the dive recovery and set the pitch attitude required to stop the deviation. The altitude was then held steadily.
texts.4: SP stabilised the aircraft within a few tens of feet of the intended recovery altitude on every entry. SP anticipated the level-off during the dive recovery and arrived at the altitude with no overshoot. Altitude control after recovery was essentially exact.
texts.marginal: SP levelled off within standards but consistently on the low side of the intended recovery altitude, correcting back each time. The deviations stayed inside the tolerance and were self-corrected. SP is expected to anticipate the level-off earlier so the altitude is captured directly.

texts_at.0: SP leveled the aircraft at the recovery altitude with the IP calling the altimeter and the pitch attitude required, since capturing an assigned altitude straight out of a dive recovery has not yet been flown without that guidance. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to check the altimeter and set the level-off pitch independently on the next recovery.
texts_at.1: SP established level flight with a deviation of about 300 feet from the intended recovery altitude, at the outer edge of the standard, due to an altimeter check made only after the pitch attitude had already been set rather than as the dive recovery began. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to bring the altimeter into the cross-check earlier in the recovery so the level-off is captured closer to the reference.
texts_at.2: SP overshot the intended recovery altitude by about 220 feet before returning to it, due to a level-off pitch that was set a beat after the dive recovery rather than anticipated during it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to set the level-off pitch as the dive recovery is completed rather than after it.
texts_at.3: SP established level flight within approximately 150 feet of the intended recovery altitude, due to an altimeter check that came a moment after the pitch attitude had been set rather than together with it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to fold the altimeter check into the same instant as the pitch change.

texts_above.1: SP checked the altimeter after the dive recovery and set the pitch required to establish level flight, settling within approximately 280 feet of the intended recovery altitude. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP checked the altimeter immediately after the dive recovery on every entry and set the pitch attitude required so the level-off settled within about 180 feet of the intended recovery altitude, comfortably inside the standard. Anticipating the level-off a moment earlier in the recovery would tighten that figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured altitude capture.
texts_above.3: SP anticipated the level-off during the dive recovery on every entry and arrived at the intended recovery altitude within about 60 feet with no overshoot to correct. The only refinement available was to fold the altimeter check into the pitch change itself rather than a moment after it. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise altitude control.
texts_above.4: SP stabilised the aircraft within a few tens of feet of the intended recovery altitude on every entry, anticipating the level-off during the dive recovery so there was no overshoot to correct. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to first-rate altitude capture.

texts.0: SP did not stabilise the airspeed after the recovery, due to power being left unmanaged through the dive and the level-off. SP allowed the airspeed to deviate more than 20 knots from the target and made no correction as the trend continued. IP took the aircraft and set the required power.
texts.1: SP stabilised at approximately 20 knots from the target airspeed after the recovery, due to a late power application during the level-off. SP corrected only after the IP called the airspeed, and the correction itself was made in coarse power changes. The airspeed settled at the limit of the acceptable band.
texts.2: SP allowed the airspeed to deviate between 10 and 20 knots from the target after the recovery, due to power being restored slightly late during the level-off. SP recognised the trend on the airspeed indicator and adjusted power in time to bring it back on its own. The airspeed then remained steady.
texts.3: SP stabilised the airspeed within 10 knots of the target after the recovery. SP restored power at the correct point in the level-off and coordinated it with the pitch change. Airspeed was held steadily in level flight.
texts.4: SP recovered to the target airspeed with only negligible deviation, holding it within a few knots throughout. SP set the power at the exact point required so that airspeed and attitude stabilised together. Speed control after recovery was precise on every repetition.
texts.marginal: SP held the airspeed within standards after the recovery but the deviations were repeatedly toward the fast side, requiring a power reduction each time. The values stayed inside tolerance and the corrections were prompt. SP is expected to set the level-off power earlier so the target speed is captured without correction.

texts_at.0: SP stabilized the airspeed after the recovery with the IP calling for the power required, since matching power to the pitch change through a dive recovery has not yet been practiced without that call. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to set the power for level flight independently on the next recovery.
texts_at.1: SP stabilised at approximately 20 knots from the target airspeed after the recovery, at the outer edge of the standard, due to a power restoration that began only once the pitch had already settled in level flight rather than during the transition to it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to begin restoring power as the pitch changes rather than after it has changed.
texts_at.2: SP allowed the airspeed to deviate by about 15 knots from the target after the recovery, due to a power change sized correctly but applied a moment after the pitch change rather than together with it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to move the throttle in the same instant as the pitch input during the level-off.
texts_at.3: SP stabilised the airspeed within approximately 10 knots of the target after the recovery, due to a power adjustment that trailed the pitch change by a beat rather than matching it exactly. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to move power and pitch together so no small chase remains.

texts_above.1: SP restored power after the dive recovery and stabilized in level flight, holding the airspeed to approximately 18 knots from the target. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP moved the throttle with the pitch input on every recovery and held the post-recovery airspeed within about 15 knots of the level-flight reference, comfortably inside the standard with no secondary correction required. Leading the power change by a fraction earlier on the fastest recoveries would tighten that figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent power management.
texts_above.3: SP anticipated the airspeed effect of each recovery and set the power accordingly, holding the post-recovery airspeed within a few knots of the level-flight reference with no overshoot in either direction. The technique is already sound; nothing in the throttle timing needs to change. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to disciplined power-to-pitch coordination.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated the airspeed effect of every attitude and set the power accordingly, holding the post-recovery airspeed essentially on the level-flight reference with no secondary throttle correction on any entry. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless power management.

texts.0: SP did not roll out on the intended exit heading, due to spatial disorientation carried over from the rotation. SP lost the reference completely, made no attempt to use the heading indicator and finished more than 10 degrees off, still turning. IP took the aircraft to establish the correct heading.
texts.1: SP rolled out approximately 10 degrees from the intended exit heading, due to disorientation following the spin that delayed the transfer of attention to the heading indicator. SP re-established the reference and corrected only after being told the heading by the IP. The correction was late and made in a single coarse turn.
texts.2: SP rolled out between 5 and 10 degrees from the intended exit heading, due to a brief disorientation after the rotation stopped. SP cross-checked the heading indicator, recognised the error and turned back onto the intended heading without any prompt. The correction was smooth and timely.
texts.3: SP rolled out within 5 degrees of the intended exit heading. SP re-established the visual and instrument references immediately after the rotation stopped and stopped the turn on the required heading. The heading was then maintained accurately.
texts.4: SP rolled out essentially on the intended exit heading on every recovery, with only a degree or two of deviation. SP retained orientation throughout the rotation and anticipated the rollout point. Heading control after recovery was exact and repeatable.
texts.marginal: SP rolled out within standards but consistently short of the intended exit heading, requiring a small correcting turn each time. The deviations remained inside tolerance and were corrected without prompting. SP is expected to anticipate the rollout so the exit heading is captured directly on the next sortie.

texts_at.0: SP rolled out on the exit heading with the IP calling the heading indicator through the last part of the rotation, since re-establishing a heading reference straight out of a spin has not yet been flown unaided. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to pick up the heading indicator independently before the rotation fully stops on the next entry.
texts_at.1: SP rolled out with a deviation of about 10 degrees from the intended exit heading, at the outer edge of the standard, due to a heading indicator cross-check made only after the rotation had already stopped rather than during the last part of it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to bring the heading indicator into the cross-check before the rotation fully stops.
texts_at.2: SP rolled out with the deviation from the intended exit heading held to about 7 degrees, due to a cross-check of the heading indicator that came a beat after the rotation stopped rather than in anticipation of it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to anticipate the exit heading during the final part of the rotation rather than checking it afterward.
texts_at.3: SP rolled out within approximately 5 degrees of the intended exit heading, due to a reference re-established a fraction after the rotation stopped rather than through the last part of it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to hold the visual and instrument references through the final part of the rotation.

texts_above.1: SP re-established the heading reference after the rotation stopped, rolling out within approximately 9 degrees of the intended exit heading. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP re-established the visual and instrument references immediately after the rotation stopped on every entry, rolling out within about 7 degrees of the intended exit heading. Picking up the reference a moment before the rotation fully stops would tighten that figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable heading recovery.

The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to very good control positioning.
texts_above.4: SP established full opposite rudder and forward of neutral stick immediately and held them positively until rotation ceased on every recovery, identifying the spin direction without hesitation and not beginning the dive recovery until the aircraft had stopped spinning. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to outstanding control positioning.

error_modes.label: STEADY STATE SPIN RECOGNITION AND RECOVERY INITIATION AT STABILISED AIRSPEED
error_modes.source: technique:6.14 INTENTIONAL SPIN ENTRY (emphasizing steady state spin recognition and recovery)

texts.0: SP did not recognise the steady state spin, due to counting turns instead of assessing the spin characteristics of 18 plus AOA, turn needle deflection and an almost constant airspeed and rotation rate. SP called for recovery at an arbitrary turn count while the airspeed was still varying, so the recovery was initiated outside the 120 to 135 KIAS window and the spin was not in the required condition. IP took the aircraft and terminated the maneuver.
texts.1: SP identified the steady state spin only at the limit of what is acceptable, due to relying on turn count rather than on the AOA and turn needle indications. SP initiated the Erect Spin Recovery at the edge of the 120 to 135 KIAS band and only after the IP called the stabilised airspeed. The recovery itself was flown correctly.
texts.2: SP was late in recognising the steady state condition, due to concentrating on the outside picture instead of cross-checking AOA, turn needle and airspeed. SP picked up the almost constant airspeed and rotation rate without prompting and initiated the recovery inside the 120 to 135 KIAS band. The spin characteristics were then correctly described.
texts.3: SP recognised the steady state spin from 18 plus AOA, turn needle deflection and the almost constant airspeed and rotation rate, and initiated the Erect Spin Recovery when the airspeed stabilised at 120 to 135 KIAS. SP treated the characteristics rather than the turn count as the cue. The recovery was started at the correct point.
texts.4: SP identified the steady state spin from its characteristics on every entry and called them as they appeared, initiating the recovery at the moment the airspeed stabilised in the 120 to 135 KIAS band. SP never referred to turn count as the criterion. Recognition and recovery initiation were consistent across all repetitions.
texts.marginal: SP recognised the steady state spin correctly but the calls came late in the stabilised airspeed band and leaned on turn count as a cross-check. Recovery was initiated within the 120 to 135 KIAS window each time. SP is expected to lead the recognition with AOA, turn needle and rotation rate rather than turns completed.

texts_at.0: SP identified the steady state spin with the IP calling out the AOA, the turn needle and the airspeed indications in turn, since reading those three cues together as one picture has not yet been practiced without that call. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to read the steady state indications independently on the next entry rather than from the call.
texts_at.1: SP recognised the steady state spin from its characteristics and initiated the Erect Spin Recovery within the 120 to 135 KIAS band on every entry, due to the airspeed being cross-checked only after the AOA and turn needle had already confirmed the steady state rather than alongside them. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to bring airspeed into the same cross-check as AOA and turn needle rather than confirming it afterward.
texts_at.2: SP recognised the steady state spin from AOA, turn needle and rotation rate on every entry and initiated the recovery inside the 120 to 135 KIAS band, due to the description of the characteristics coming a beat after they were first read rather than as they were read. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to call the characteristics in the same moment they are recognised.
texts_at.3: SP recognised the steady state spin from 18 plus AOA, turn needle deflection and the almost constant airspeed and rotation rate on every entry, due to the airspeed stabilising being confirmed a moment after the other two indications rather than together with them. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to fold all three indications into a single cross-check.

texts_above.1: SP recognized the steady state spin from the AOA and turn needle indications, initiating the recovery after being called for the stabilised airspeed within the 120 to 135 KIAS band. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP picked up the almost constant airspeed and rotation rate on every entry and initiated the recovery inside the 120 to 135 KIAS band without relying on turn count, treating the characteristics rather than the count as the cue each time. Calling the characteristics aloud as they are read would sharpen the cross-check further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady spin-characteristic recognition.
texts_above.3: SP treated the characteristics rather than the turn count as the cue on every entry and initiated the Erect Spin Recovery precisely as the airspeed stabilised in the 120 to 135 KIAS band each time. The only refinement available was to call each characteristic aloud as it is recognised. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed spin-characteristic recognition.
texts_above.4: SP identified the steady state spin from its characteristics on every entry and called them as they appeared, initiating the recovery at the moment the airspeed stabilised in the 120 to 135 KIAS band with no reference to turn count at any point. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exemplary spin-characteristic recognition.
